newsitem.title: USA: US steel mills face "profitless prosperity".
newsitem.headline: US steel mills face "profitless prosperity".

text.p: The U.S. steel industry appears headed for another period of "profitless prosperity" in the near term as the market becomes increasingly competitive despite good demand, Robert Wendt of the Millbrook Group said.
"We have lost forward momentum and propulsion," Wendt told Ryan's Notes conference on vanadium, molybdenum and columbium - three ferro-alloys used in steelmaking.

"We are on the cusp of a major shift in buyer psychology. The 1997 market will become increasingly competitive and there is a very high risk of further erosion for the steel industry's financial performance," Wendt added.

Key steel consuming sectors of auto, construction and machinery would see demand flat or lower in the near term. The intensity of steel's use in the U.S. economy has also reached a plateau in the current cycle.
Auto making was expected to remain at 14.5 to 15 million units a year in the U.S.
"Overall, we expect a slight, 1 percent decline in steel consumption in the economy in 1997," Wendt said. Demand this year will be 110 million tons.
The bottom of the cycle will be reached in 1998, with a recovery in the market from the end of the following year.
U.S. steel supply exceeded demand by 5 million tons last year when consumption totaled 111 million tons. Demand in 1998 and 1999 was expected to total 108 million and 111 million tons respectively.
"The bad news is the potential for excess supply and an extremely positive market that will be remembered as another period of 'profitless prosperity'", Wendt said.
